name: Cognitive Restructuring
description: Identifying an automatic negative thought, examining the evidence for and against it, and replacing it with a more balanced, realistic thought.
citation: Beck, A. T. (1979). Cognitive Therapy of Depression. Guilford Press.
limitations: Requires enough self-reflective capacity to separate a thought from a fact; not a substitute for treatment of clinical depression.

name: Decatastrophizing ("What If" Technique)
description: Walking through the actually-likely outcome, the worst-case outcome, and how one would cope with the worst case, to reduce the perceived unbearability of a feared event.
citation: Beck, A. T., Emery, G., & Greenberg, R. L. (1985). Anxiety Disorders and Phobias: A Cognitive Perspective. Basic Books.
limitations: Can feel invalidating if used before the person feels heard; should follow, not replace, emotional validation.

name: Behavioral Activation
description: Scheduling small, concrete, achievable activities (especially ones tied to values or past enjoyment) to counteract withdrawal and low mood, rather than waiting to 'feel like it' first.
citation: Jacobson, N. S., Dobson, K. S., Truax, P. A., et al. (1996). A component analysis of cognitive-behavioral treatment for depression. Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology, 64(2), 295-304.
limitations: Effortful to start precisely when motivation is lowest; works best with very small first steps.

name: Self-Compassion Practice
description: Responding to one's own suffering or perceived failure with the same kindness, warmth, and understanding one would offer a good friend, rather than harsh self-judgment.
citation: Neff, K. D. (2003). Self-compassion: An alternative conceptualization of a healthy attitude toward oneself. Self and Identity, 2(2), 85-101.
limitations: Can initially feel unfamiliar or 'soft' to people used to self-criticism as a motivator; benefits usually build with repeated practice.

name: Values Clarification (ACT)
description: Distinguishing what genuinely matters to the person (their values) from the anxious thought itself, then identifying one small action in line with that value regardless of the discomfort.
citation: Hayes, S. C., Strosahl, K. D., & Wilson, K. G. (1999). Acceptance and Commitment Therapy: An Experiential Approach to Behavior Change. Guilford Press.
limitations: Not aimed at eliminating the anxious thought, which can be unsatisfying for someone wanting the thought itself to go away.

name: Behavioral Experiment
description: Turning a feared prediction into a small, testable real-world experiment (e.g. 'if I ask, they will say no') to gather actual evidence instead of relying on assumption.
citation: Bennett-Levy, J., Butler, G., Fennell, M., et al. (2004). Oxford Guide to Behavioural Experiments in Cognitive Therapy. Oxford University Press.
limitations: Needs a genuinely testable, low-stakes prediction; not suitable for high-risk or irreversible situations.

name: Gratitude Practice
description: Deliberately noticing and recording a small number of specific positive things, which has been shown to shift attention away from a purely deficit-focused view of one's life.
citation: Emmons, R. A., & McCullough, M. E. (2003). Counting blessings versus burdens: An experimental investigation of gratitude and subjective well-being. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 84(2), 377-389.
limitations: Not appropriate as a first response to acute distress; can read as dismissive if offered too early.

name: Structured Problem-Solving
description: Breaking an overwhelming situation into a defined problem, a brainstormed list of options, a chosen option, and one concrete next action, to counter paralysis in the face of a large stressor.
citation: D'Zurilla, T. J., & Nezu, A. M. (2007). Problem-Solving Therapy: A Positive Approach to Clinical Intervention (3rd ed.). Springer.
limitations: Less useful when the core issue is an internal emotional state rather than an external, actionable problem.

name: Checking Assumptions (Interpersonal Effectiveness)
description: Treating an assumption about what someone else is thinking as a hypothesis to check (by asking, observing, or seeking evidence) rather than as an established fact.
citation: Linehan, M. M. (1993). Cognitive-Behavioral Treatment of Borderline Personality Disorder. Guilford Press.
limitations: Directly asking isn't always possible or safe in every relationship or context; use judgment about when it's appropriate.

name: Thought Record
description: Writing down the situation, the automatic thought, the emotion, and evidence for and against the thought in a structured column format, to counter selectively noticing only the negative.
citation: Greenberger, D., & Padesky, C. A. (1995). Mind Over Mood: Change How You Feel by Changing the Way You Think. Guilford Press.
limitations: Can feel effortful or overly clinical for some people; benefits usually build with repeated practice rather than a single use.

name: Cognitive Defusion (ACT)
description: Noticing a feeling-driven thought as 'just a thought passing through' rather than as literal truth, creating enough distance from it to choose a response instead of reacting automatically.
citation: Hayes, S. C., Strosahl, K. D., & Wilson, K. G. (1999). Acceptance and Commitment Therapy: An Experiential Approach to Behavior Change. Guilford Press.
limitations: Takes practice to feel natural; can seem abstract without guided practice examples.

name: Should-to-Prefer Reframe (REBT)
description: Replacing a rigid 'should' or 'must' demand on yourself or others with a flexible preference, reducing the guilt or anger that comes from an unmet absolute rule.
citation: Ellis, A. (1962). Reason and Emotion in Psychotherapy. Lyle Stuart.
limitations: Some 'shoulds' reflect genuine values worth keeping; the goal is flexibility, not abandoning all standards.

name: Responsibility Pie
description: Listing every factor that contributed to an outcome and assigning each a realistic share of responsibility, to counter taking on 100% of the blame for events with multiple causes.
citation: Burns, D. D. (1980). Feeling Good: The New Mood Therapy. William Morrow.
limitations: Not meant to eliminate genuine accountability where it exists; the goal is an accurate share, not zero responsibility.

name: Mindful Awareness of Comparison
description: Noticing a comparison thought as it arises, without judgment, and gently redirecting attention back to one's own present experience and progress.
citation: Kabat-Zinn, J. (1990). Full Catastrophe Living. Delta.
limitations: Mindfulness skills build gradually with practice; a single attempt may not immediately reduce the comparison thought's intensity.

name: Locus of Control Mapping
description: Sorting a situation's elements into what is genuinely within your control, what you can influence, and what isn't yours to control, to counter both helplessness and over-responsibility.
citation: Rotter, J. B. (1966). Generalized expectancies for internal versus external control of reinforcement. Psychological Monographs, 80(1), 1-28.
limitations: Sorting can be genuinely difficult in ambiguous situations where influence is real but partial.

name: Savoring
description: Deliberately slowing down to notice and absorb a positive moment -- what led to it, how it feels in the body, what it says about you -- instead of letting it pass unexamined.
citation: Bryant, F. B., & Veroff, J. (2007). Savoring: A New Model of Positive Experience. Lawrence Erlbaum Associates.
limitations: Only applicable when there is a genuine positive moment to work with; not a substitute for addressing the distortion when it recurs.

name: Broaden-and-Build Reflection
description: Using a moment of positive emotion to briefly widen attention -- what new ideas, connections, or options feel possible right now that didn't before -- and noting one worth acting on.
citation: Fredrickson, B. L. (2001). The role of positive emotions in positive psychology: The broaden-and-build theory. American Psychologist, 56(3), 218-226.
limitations: Works best as a brief reflective pause, not a forced search for silver linings in genuinely difficult situations.

name: 5-4-3-2-1 Grounding
description: Naming five things you can see, four you can hear, three you can touch, two you can smell, and one you can taste, to bring attention back to the present moment when it's been hijacked by worry.
citation: Najavits, L. M. (2002). Seeking Safety: A Treatment Manual for PTSD and Substance Abuse. Guilford Press.
limitations: Grounding reduces acute distress in the moment; it does not address the underlying thought pattern on its own.

name: Scheduled Worry Time
description: Setting aside a fixed, short daily window to deliberately think through worries, and deferring intrusive worry thoughts to that window the rest of the day.
citation: Borkovec, T. D., Wilkinson, L., Folensbee, R., & Lerman, C. (1983). Stimulus control applications to the treatment of worry. Behaviour Research and Therapy, 21(3), 247-251.
limitations: Takes a few days of practice to build the habit; not intended for acute crisis-level distress.
